We need to produce a resume for Matthias Algiers. Use words with all capital letters to highlight key abilities, but ensure that words with all capital letters appear less than 10 times. So we can have up to 9 all caps words. Must wrap entire response with double quotation marks. So output must be a string that starts and ends with a double quote character. Inside we have the resume text. Must ensure that all caps words count <10. We can use maybe 5 all caps words: e.g., LEADERSHIP, PROJECT_MANAGEMENT, DATA_ANALYSIS, COMMUNICATION, PROBLEM_SOLVING. Ensure they are all caps and separated by spaces or punctuation. Count them: each occurrence counts as a word. Need less than 10 occurrences total. We can use each once, so 5 occurrences. Good.

We must not add commentary about constraints. Just output the resume wrapped in double quotes.

We must ensure the double quotes are at very start and end, and not include extra whitespace outside? Probably fine.

We need to embed all caps words for key abilities. Use them within sentences.

Make sure not to accidentally create other all caps words like "USA" or "SQL"? Those are also all caps and would count. Better avoid any other all caps words. So avoid acronyms like USA, SQL, HTML, etc. Use lowercase for those or avoid them. Use "sql" lowercase. Avoid "USA". Use "United States". Avoid "CEO". Use lowercase.

Thus we need to watch out for any accidental all caps like "I" is a single letter capital but not a word? "I" is a word, all caps? It's a single capital letter; it's considered a word with all caps? Probably yes, "I" is all caps. But we cannot avoid using "I" in resume? We could avoid first-person pronouns; use third person or omit pronouns. Use bullet points starting with action verbs, no "I". So we can avoid "I". Also avoid "A" as a word? "A" is capital letter but it's a word; it's all caps? It's a single capital letter; but it's a word. If we use "A" as article, it's capitalized only at start of sentence; but if we start sentences with capital letter, the first word will be capitalized but not all caps unless the whole word is uppercase. So "A" as first letter capital but rest lowercase? Actually "A" is just one letter; if it's capitalized, it's uppercase letter; there is no lowercase version. So "A" is effectively all caps. That would be problematic. Many sentences start with "A". To avoid that, we can avoid starting sentences with "A". But we can't avoid using "a" as article mid-sentence; it will be lowercase. So we must ensure we don't have any standalone capital "A". Starting a sentence with "An" also capital A but it's not all caps because it's "An": first letter capital, second lowercase; not all caps. So only words that are all uppercase letters count. So "A" as a single uppercase letter counts as all caps word. So we must avoid using the word "A" as a standalone word. Similarly "I". So we need to avoid those. That is tricky but doable: we can avoid using the article "a" altogether? We can use "an" instead of "a" when needed, but "an" also starts with vowel; but we need to use indefinite article sometimes. We can avoid using "a" by rephrasing: use "one" or "the". Use "the" instead of "a". So we can avoid "a". Also avoid "I". Use passive voice or start sentences with verbs.

We also need to avoid other accidental all caps like "USA", "UK", "CEO", "CFO", "AI", "IT". We'll avoid those.

We need to ensure that our all caps highlighted words are less than 10. We'll pick maybe 6: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC_THINKING, DATA_ANALYSIS, PROJECT_MANAGEMENT, COMMUNICATION, PROBLEM_SOLVING. Ensure they have underscores or no spaces? Underscore counts as part of word; still all caps if letters are uppercase and underscores are not letters; but the word includes underscores; still considered a word? Probably yes, but it's still all caps letters plus underscores; but underscores are not letters, but the definition of "words with all capital letters" likely means tokens consisting only of uppercase letters (A-Z). Underscore might break that. Safer to use plain uppercase words without punctuation: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGICTHINKING? That's weird. Better to use camel case? Not allowed. We could use hyphen? Hyphen not letter. Might still be considered not all caps. Safer to use plain uppercase words: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC, DATAANALYSIS? Hmm.

We can just use single words: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC, ANALYSIS, PROJECT, COMMUNICATION, SOLVING. But those may be ambiguous. Better to use compound words without spaces but still all letters uppercase: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGICTHINKING, DATA ANALYSIS can't have space. Use "DATAANALYSIS". That's all caps letters. Similarly "PROJECTMANAGEMENT". "COMMUNICATION". "PROBLEMSOLVING". That yields 6 words.

Check each: LEADERSHIP (all caps), STRATEGICTHINKING (all caps), DATAANALYSIS (all caps), PROJECTMANAGEMENT (all caps), COMMUNICATION (all caps), PROBLEMSOLVING (all caps). That's 6.

Now ensure we don't accidentally have other all caps like "THE"? "THE" is all caps if we write it uppercase. We'll avoid writing "THE" as all caps; we will write "the" lowercase. So we need to be careful not to accidentally uppercase any word. We'll write all sentences in normal case, with first letter capitalized only for start of sentence. But we must ensure that we don't accidentally have words like "I" as a pronoun. We'll avoid using "I". We'll also avoid using "A" as article; we will use "an" or "the". "An" starts with capital A if at start of sentence; but we can avoid starting sentences with "An". We'll start sentences with verbs or proper nouns like "Matthias". That's okay: "Matthias" capital M, rest lowercase, not all caps. Good.

We need to watch for "US" if we write "United States". That's "US" as abbreviation? We'll write "United States" fully, not abbreviation. So "United" capital U, rest lowercase; "States" capital S, rest lowercase. Not all caps.

We need to avoid "LLC", "Inc." etc. We'll avoid.

Now construct resume.

We'll wrap entire response with double quotation marks. So output starts with ", ends with ". Inside we have resume text, with line breaks allowed? Probably yes. The double quotes at start and end must be the only ones? It says wrap the entire response with double quotation marks. So we output a string that begins with " and ends with ". Inside we can have line breaks. That is fine.
